lessons.title: Points, angles and plane figures
lessons.summary: Read geometric labels and recognise triangles, special quadrilaterals and named polygons.
lessons.objective: Read geometric labels and recognise triangles, special quadrilaterals and named polygons.
lessons.before: Read a diagram by following its labels and markings.
lessons.ideas:
In \(\angle ABC\), the middle letter B is the vertex. An acute angle is below \(90^\circ\), an obtuse angle is between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), and a reflex angle is between \(180^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\). The right angle is \(90^\circ\).

Square: four equal sides and four right angles. Rectangle: four right angles. Rhombus: four equal sides. Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides. Parallelogram: two pairs of parallel sides. A trapezium has a pair of parallel sides.

Parallel lines in a plane stay the same distance apart. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. In Extended vocabulary, a plane is a flat surface and a perpendicular bisector crosses a segment at its midpoint at right angles.
lessons.method:
Which point is the vertex of the angle?

A point marks an exact position. A vertex is a corner where two sides or rays meet. A line segment joins two endpoints.

How do I tell these triangles and quadrilaterals apart?

Check triangle side marks first. An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, an isosceles triangle has at least two, and a scalene triangle has three different sides. A right-angled triangle has one right angle.

How do I recognise regular polygons and line relationships?

Regular means all sides and all angles are equal. A pentagon has 5 sides, a hexagon 6, an octagon 8 and a decagon 10. Interior angles lie inside. An exterior angle is formed at a vertex by extending a side.
mistakes: The first or last letter lies on a ray. It is not the vertex unless it is the middle letter.
A square also meets the definitions of rectangle and rhombus. When a question asks for the most specific label, use square.
Equal side lengths alone do not make every polygon regular. A rhombus can have two different angles.

examples.title: Read the middle letter of an angle
examples.question:
Which point is the vertex of \(\angle ABC\)?

  1. A
  2. B
  3. C
  4. D
examples.solution:
Read the three-letter name in order. The middle letter is B.

The two sides of the angle meet at B.

examples.title: Recognise a triangle from its markings
examples.question:
All sides have the same length. Choose the most informative type for the stated property.

  1. Equilateral
  2. Isosceles with exactly two equal sides
  3. Scalene with no right angle
  4. Right-angled
examples.solution:
All sides have the same length.

This identifies the equilateral triangle.

examples.title: Name a polygon from the number of sides
examples.question:
A polygon has 5 equal sides and all its angles are equal. What is its name?

  1. Regular pentagon
  2. Regular hexagon
  3. Regular octagon
  4. Regular decagon
examples.solution:
The number of sides is 5, which gives a pentagon.

With equal sides and equal angles, it is regular.

lessons.title: Solids and circle vocabulary
lessons.summary: Name solids and distinguish the parts and regions of a circle.
lessons.objective: Name solids and distinguish the parts and regions of a circle.
lessons.before: A face, edge and vertex describe different parts of a solid.
lessons.ideas:
A cylinder has two equal circular ends. A pyramid's triangular faces meet at an apex. A cone has a circular base and an apex. Each boundary point of a sphere is the same distance from its centre.

A diameter is a chord passing through the centre. A tangent touches the circle at one point. A semicircle is one half of the circle divided by a diameter.

A net is a flat arrangement that folds into a solid. For Extended, the shorter arc between two points is the minor arc and the longer is the major arc, where the lengths differ. A hemisphere is half a sphere. A frustum remains after a smaller similar top is removed parallel to the base.
lessons.method:
Which features identify the solid?

Compare faces, surfaces and cross-sections. A cube has six square faces. A cuboid has rectangular faces. A prism keeps the same cross-section along its length.

Which points does a circle feature join?

The centre is inside. The circumference is the full outer curve. A radius joins the centre to the curve. A chord joins two points on the circumference.

What encloses a sector or segment?

An arc is part of the circumference. A sector is enclosed by two radii and an arc. A segment is enclosed by a chord and an arc.
mistakes: Only the flat parts are faces in these descriptions. A cylinder or cone also has a curved surface.
An ordinary chord may lie anywhere across a circle. It does not have to pass through the centre.
A sector reaches the centre. A minor segment bounded by a chord that misses the centre does not reach the centre.

examples.title: Identify a solid from its defining features
examples.question:
Name a solid with this description. A solid with six equal square faces.

  1. Cube
  2. Cuboid
  3. Triangular prism
  4. Cylinder
examples.solution: Look for the combination of faces and surfaces. The stated features belong to a cube.

examples.title: Identify a straight circle feature
examples.question:
Name the highlighted straight feature on the circle.

  1. Radius
  2. Diameter
  3. Chord (not a diameter)
examples.solution:
It joins the centre to the circumference.

The most specific name is radius.

examples.title: Use circle vocabulary precisely
examples.question:
Which term describes one half of the circular region divided by a diameter?

  1. Semicircle
  2. Circumference
  3. Major arc (Extended)
  4. Minor arc (Extended)
examples.solution: The words identify semicircle.

lessons.title: Measure and construct with ruler and compasses
lessons.summary: Measure and draw lines and angles, and use two compass arcs to construct a triangle from three side lengths.
lessons.objective: Measure and draw lines and angles, and use two compass arcs to construct a triangle from three side lengths.
lessons.before: Distinguish a ruler, a pair of compasses and a protractor.
lessons.ideas:
To draw an angle, mark its value on that same scale. Use a ruler to join the mark to the vertex. To draw a line of a given length, place the ruler zero at the start and mark the required endpoint.

Set the compasses to AC and draw an arc centred at A. Reset to BC and draw an intersecting arc centred at B. Join the crossing to A and B with a ruler.

Leave both arc crossings, one on each side of the diagonal. Joining each crossing to both ends gives four equal sides. Ruler-and-compass constructions show the distances directly.
lessons.method:
Where do I put the protractor?

Place the marked centre of the protractor at the vertex. Align its zero line with the starting arm. Read the scale that starts at zero on that arm.

How do I select both compass radii?

Draw AB to its stated length. The third vertex C lies the given distance from A and the given distance from B.

How do I complete a rhombus or check a drawing?

Start with one diagonal of the rhombus. The other two vertices are each a side length away from both ends of that diagonal.
mistakes: Using the opposite protractor scale can swap an acute angle with its supplementary obtuse angle.
Measuring an angle to guess C does not show that the third side has the stated length.
On a phone, the size of the displayed diagram can change. Use the reference bar when reading a length from a digital diagram and a physical ruler when drawing at a specified length.

examples.title: Measure an angle from the correct baseline
examples.question: Measure the marked smaller angle to the nearest degree. Treat the horizontal ray to the right as the starting ray.
examples.solution:
Centre the protractor on P. Align the zero line with the ray going right.

Read the scale that starts at zero on that arm. The angle is \(37^\circ\).

examples.title: Read a length from a calibrated diagram
examples.question: The reference bar represents 1 cm. Read the length of AB without relying on the size displayed on your screen.
examples.solution:
There are 3 equal divisions along AB.

Each is the length of the reference bar. The represented length is \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Use both compass arcs for the third vertex
examples.question:
In a ruler-and-compasses SSS construction of ABC with \(AB=5\), \(AC=4\) and \(BC=6\) centimetres, where should C be marked?

  1. At the crossing of the two required arcs
  2. At the midpoint of AB
  3. At any point on the first arc
examples.solution:
Draw AB with length \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Use radius \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\) at A and radius \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) at B.

Their intersection is C. Draw AC and BC with the ruler and keep the arcs.

lessons.title: Draw and use nets of solids
lessons.summary: Match flat arrangements to solids, draw compatible faces and use net measurements to find surface area or volume.
lessons.objective: Match flat arrangements to solids, draw compatible faces and use net measurements to find surface area or volume.
lessons.before: Recognise common triangles, rectangles and squares. Check which edges have the same length.
lessons.ideas:
For a triangular prism, identify two matching triangle ends and the three rectangular sides. A square-based pyramid has a square base and four triangles that meet at the apex.

For a rectangular prism, a strip of four side faces can wrap around. Attach the two matching end faces so they close the opposite ends. For a square pyramid, attach one triangle to each side of the square.

For a prism volume, identify one end area and its perpendicular distance from the matching end. Multiply those and report cubic units.
lessons.method:
How do I predict the folded shape?

A cube net has six equal squares. A cuboid net uses three pairs of equal rectangles. Edges that join when folded must have the same length.

How do I draw a net that will close?

Draw one face using the stated lengths. Add the adjacent faces along edges they share. Check each joining length before drawing the next face.

How do I use the measurements from the net?

Surface area is the sum of the areas of every face on the net. Count all equal copies and keep square units.
mistakes: Six faces with the right individual shapes can still fold to an overlap if they are arranged badly.
The sloping height within a triangular face of a pyramid is not the perpendicular height of the whole pyramid.
Adding all the face areas gives surface area. It does not give the volume.

examples.title: Match a net to the solid it forms
examples.question:
Name the solid formed by folding this net.

  1. Cube
  2. Cuboid with unequal edges
  3. Triangular prism
  4. Square-based pyramid
examples.solution:
Six congruent squares fold to the six faces.

The folded shape is a cube.

examples.title: Match a net to the solid it forms
examples.question:
Name the solid formed by folding this net.

  1. Cube
  2. Cuboid with unequal edges
  3. Triangular prism
  4. Square-based pyramid
examples.solution:
Two matching triangular bases and three rectangles make the prism.

The folded shape is a triangular prism.

examples.title: Find volume from a prism net
examples.question: A triangular-prism net has two right-angled triangles with perpendicular sides 3 cm and 4 cm. Each rectangular side is 4 cm along the prism. Find the volume.
examples.solution:
The area of each triangular end is \(\frac12\times3\times4\) square centimetres, or \(6\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

Multiply the end area by the prism length. The volume is \(24\,\mathrm{cm^3}\).

lessons.title: Scale drawings and three-figure bearings
lessons.summary: Convert drawing distances both ways, measure clockwise from north and plot routes with ruler and protractor.
lessons.objective: Convert drawing distances both ways, measure clockwise from north and plot routes with ruler and protractor.
lessons.before: Recall that 100 cm make 1 m and 1000 m make 1 km.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply the drawing length to find the real distance. Divide the real distance to find the length to draw. For a ratio scale, express both lengths in the same unit first.

Write the bearing with three digits. North is \(000^\circ\), east \(090^\circ\), south \(180^\circ\) and west \(270^\circ\).

Mark the endpoint along that ray using its scaled distance. To reverse a bearing, add half a turn and subtract \(360^\circ\) if the result reaches a full turn.
lessons.method:
When do I multiply or divide by the scale?

A scale connects a drawing length with the real length it represents. Write down what one centimetre represents before starting.

Where do I start measuring a bearing?

In ‘B from A’, stand at A. Draw a north arrow at A and measure clockwise to the route AB.

How do I draw a route and find its reverse bearing?

First convert the real length to the drawing length. Set the protractor centre at the starting point and mark the clockwise angle.
mistakes: A scale of 1 : 500 compares centimetres with centimetres. It does not say one centimetre on the plan stands for 500 metres.
The shortest angle from north may go anticlockwise. The bearing still uses the complete clockwise turn.
Swapping the names of the points without changing the measurement leaves the original direction.

examples.title: Convert a scale-drawing length to a real distance
examples.question: A plan uses 1 cm to represent 3 m. A path measures 2 cm on the plan. Find its real length in metres.
examples.solution:
Each of the 2 centimetres stands for 3 metres.

Multiply 2 by 3. The real distance is \(6\,\mathrm{m}\).

examples.title: Convert the units in a ratio scale
examples.question: A model uses the scale 1 : 300. A real length is 6 m. What is its model length in centimetres?
examples.solution:
The scale compares the same units. Convert 6 m to 600 cm.

Divide by 300. The model length is \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Find a reverse bearing
examples.question: The bearing of B from A is \(024^\circ\). Find the bearing of A from B.
examples.solution:
The reverse route points in exactly the opposite direction.

Add a half-turn of \(180^\circ\). If needed, subtract a full turn. The bearing is \(204^\circ\).

lessons.title: Corresponding sides of similar shapes
lessons.summary: Match like sides, choose the direction of the scale factor and find missing lengths.
lessons.objective: Match like sides, choose the direction of the scale factor and find missing lengths.
lessons.before: Congruent shapes have the same shape and size. Similar shapes have the same shape. They can differ in size.
lessons.ideas:
A shape may be turned over or rotated. Follow the same marked angles and endpoints, then pair the sides that join them.

A factor greater than one gives an enlargement. A factor between zero and one gives a reduction. Apply the same factor to every matching length.

Divide by the enlargement factor to reverse an enlargement. You can instead multiply by the reciprocal factor. Both approaches use the same matching sides.
lessons.method:
Which sides actually correspond?

The same angle positions and same relative lengths identify corresponding sides. When names are given in corresponding order, match the first letters, second letters and third letters.

Which length goes on top of the factor?

Use one complete pair of corresponding sides. Take the target length over the starting length.

How do I work back to the smaller shape?

A factor describes one direction. If a known factor takes small to large, the inverse goes from large to small.
mistakes: The leftmost sides on two pictures need not correspond. Check geometric markings or the stated order.
Using a ratio of two sides of different types can give a number with no scale-factor meaning.
It is easy to apply the same enlargement factor again when trying to recover an original length.

examples.title: Match sides using the order of the vertices
examples.question:
Triangles ABC and PQR are similar, with vertices in corresponding order. Which side of PQR corresponds to AC?

  1. PR
  2. PQ
  3. QR
examples.solution:
Match each vertex to the letter at the same position in the other name.

The corresponding side is PR.

examples.title: Find a missing length in a larger similar triangle
examples.question: Two similar triangles have corresponding bases 6 cm and 9 cm. A different small side is 10 cm. Find the matching large side.
examples.solution:
The enlargement multiplies lengths by \(\frac{3}{2}\).

Multiply \(10\) by that factor to get \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Use the same scale factor across a third side
examples.question: Triangles ABC and PQR are similar in that order. AB = 6 cm, PQ = 9 cm and AC = 14 cm. Find PR.
examples.solution:
AB corresponds to PQ. The length factor from ABC to PQR is \(\frac{3}{2}\).

AC corresponds to PR. Multiplying gives \(21\,\mathrm{cm}\).

lessons.title: Similarity reasons, areas and volumes (Extended)
lessons.summary: Explain why triangles are similar, apply the square and cube scale laws and recover lengths from area or volume ratios.
lessons.objective: Explain why triangles are similar, apply the square and cube scale laws and recover lengths from area or volume ratios.
lessons.before: Find a length scale factor by dividing a pair of corresponding lengths.
lessons.ideas:
Give a reason for each pair. A shared angle, a right-angle mark or equal angles in parallel lines can identify correspondence. Two angles establish similarity, but the sizes can differ.

If lengths scale by \(k\), areas scale by \(k^2\). The surface areas of similar solids obey the same rule because each matching face or patch is two-dimensional.

A length factor \(k\) gives volume factor \(k^3\). To reverse this, divide the volumes to get their factor and take its positive cube root. Then compare corresponding lengths.
lessons.method:
When are two matching angles enough?

Two matching angle pairs in triangles are enough for similarity. The final pair also matches because every triangle has total interior angle \(180^\circ\).

Why is the area factor squared?

Lengths scale by the same factor in both directions in a similar plane shape.

How do I find length from a volume comparison?

Volume changes along three perpendicular directions, all by the same factor.
mistakes: One right angle in each triangle is insufficient. You need a second matching angle or another valid similarity argument.
The length multiplier does not directly multiply an area. To find the length factor from an area ratio, take its positive square root.
Using the square root of a volume ratio would undo only a change in two dimensions.

examples.title: Justify similarity using two angles
examples.question:
Each of two triangles has a right angle and an angle of \(31^\circ\). Which fact proves they are similar?

  1. Two corresponding angles are equal
  2. Their longest sides are the same length
  3. Both triangles have the same area
  4. One pair of corresponding angles is equal
examples.solution:
The right angles match and the two angles of \(31^\circ\) match.

Two matching angle pairs establish similarity. The third pair matches from the triangle angle sum.

examples.title: Recover a length factor from a pair of areas
examples.question: Two similar shapes have areas \(24\,\mathrm{cm^2}\) and \(54\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Find the length scale factor from smaller to larger.
examples.solution:
The area scale factor is \(\frac{9}{4}\).

Take its positive square root to obtain \(\frac{3}{2}\). Lengths are multiplied by the square root of the area factor.

examples.title: Find the volume after changing the scale
examples.question: Two similar solids have heights \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\). The smaller has volume \(48\,\mathrm{cm^3}\). Find the volume of the larger.
examples.solution:
The length scale factor is \(\frac{3}{2}\).

The volume factor is the cube of the length factor, giving \(\frac{27}{8}\). Multiply to obtain \(162\,\mathrm{cm^3}\).

lessons.title: Line and rotational symmetry
lessons.summary: Count true mirror lines and matching turns of plane shapes, and complete a symmetrical grid pattern.
lessons.objective: Count true mirror lines and matching turns of plane shapes, and complete a symmetrical grid pattern.
lessons.before: Know the properties of the common triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons.
lessons.ideas:
A non-square rectangle has two lines along its midlines. A square also has two diagonal mirror lines. A usual kite with unequal pairs of sides has one mirror line.

A regular \(n\)-sided polygon has \(n\) matches. The first positive matching angle is \(\frac{360^\circ}{n}\). A shape with no earlier match has order one.

With a vertical mirror, both copies stay in the same row. With a horizontal mirror, both stay in the same column.
lessons.method:
Which lines reflect the whole shape onto itself?

Reflecting a shape across a line of symmetry places each vertex, edge and marked feature directly on a matching one.

How do I count matching positions in a turn?

The order is the number of matches in one full turn about the centre. Count the return to the starting orientation once.

How do I complete a mirror pattern accurately?

On a grid, find the nearest point on the mirror to each shaded cell. Copy the cell to the other side at the same distance.
mistakes: A rectangle's diagonal gives two triangles of equal area but does not reflect the rectangle onto itself unless the rectangle is square.
Count only exact matches of all features. A half-turn does not give the same shape if a decoration or unequal side moves to a different position.
Translating a cell by a fixed number of spaces does not reflect cells whose distances from the mirror differ.

examples.title: Count mirror lines of a plane shape
examples.question: How many lines of symmetry does the pictured square have?
examples.solution:
A flip across a valid line maps every feature to its matching position.

The square shown has 4 lines of symmetry.

examples.title: Identify mirror lines of different triangles
examples.question: How many lines of symmetry does this equilateral triangle have?
examples.solution:
Check whether reflecting across a line through a vertex swaps two equal sides.

For the triangle shown, the number of mirror lines is 3.

examples.title: Find the smallest positive matching turn
examples.question: By what smallest positive angle does a regular 5-sided polygon rotate onto itself?
examples.solution:
There are 5 equally spaced matches during a full turn.

Divide \(360^\circ\) by 5, giving \(72^\circ\).

lessons.title: Planes and axes of symmetry (Extended)
lessons.summary: Identify symmetry planes and rotation axes of prisms, cylinders, pyramids and cones.
lessons.objective: Identify symmetry planes and rotation axes of prisms, cylinders, pyramids and cones.
lessons.before: Recall a plane is a flat surface and an axis is a line.
lessons.ideas:
If an end cross-section has a mirror line, extending that line along the length can give another mirror plane. A cuboid with three different edge lengths has three central planes parallel to its faces.

A right cone also has mirror planes containing its axis through the apex and base centre. Unlike a cylinder, it has no mirror plane parallel to the base that swaps its top and bottom.

The central vertical line of a right circular cone has a match at every rotation angle. For the square pyramid, four specific rotations match during a complete turn.
lessons.method:
Which plane can swap a prism's two ends?

Every right prism has a plane halfway between its two matching ends and parallel to them. Reflection in this plane swaps the ends.

Which planes and axes fit a circular solid?

A right cylinder has a central lengthways axis through the centres of its circular ends. A mirror plane containing that axis can cut each circular cross-section along a diameter.

What creates repeating turns of a pyramid?

For a right square-based pyramid, rotate the vertical line through the apex and centre of the base. The square and its triangular faces match every quarter-turn.
mistakes: A prism's end face is not itself a mirror plane. The solid would reflect outside its original position.
A circular-looking cross-section does not mean reflection across any horizontal slice will preserve the whole solid.
A central line does not make every angular rotation a symmetry. Check the shape of the cross-section.

examples.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
examples.question:
Consider a right triangular prism with its two ends 5 cm apart. How far from one end is the mirror plane which swaps the matching ends?

  1. \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  2. \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  3. \(0\,\mathrm{cm}\)
examples.solution:
The central transverse plane is halfway between the identical ends. Their points match at equal distances across it.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

examples.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
examples.question:
Consider a right circular cylinder of height 5 cm. How far from the base is the mirror plane that swaps the two circular ends?

  1. \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  2. \(\frac{5}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}\)
  3. \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\)
examples.solution:
The two end circles lie on opposite sides of the central plane, at equal perpendicular distances.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

examples.title: Identify a solid's symmetry feature
examples.question:
Consider a right square-based pyramid whose square has side 4 cm. A turn of \(90^\circ\) about the line through its apex and base centre returns it to an identical position. What is its complete order of rotation?

  1. 4
  2. 2
  3. 1
examples.solution:
Viewed down that axis, a quarter-turn matches the base and each triangular face with the next one. There are four matches in one full turn.

The symmetry must match the entire solid, not just its outline from one view.

lessons.title: Angles at points, on lines and in shapes
lessons.summary: Choose the correct sum or equality and give geometrical reasons for unknown angles.
lessons.objective: Choose the correct sum or equality and give geometrical reasons for unknown angles.
lessons.before: In a three-letter angle name, the middle letter is its vertex.
lessons.ideas:
Identify the whole group first. Subtract every known part from its correct total. A missing reflex angle is the remaining large part of the full turn.

The three interior angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\). If one is missing, subtract the other two from that total.

A diagonal splits a convex quadrilateral into two triangles. Its four interior angles therefore sum to \(360^\circ\).
lessons.method:
Is this a straight line or a full turn?

All the angles around a point make a complete turn of \(360^\circ\). Angles that fill one side of a straight line make a half-turn of \(180^\circ\).

When are angles equal instead of supplementary?

When two straight lines cross, opposite angles have equal size. Adjacent angles on the same straight line are supplementary.

How do equal sides and diagonals help?

Two equal sides of an isosceles triangle face equal angles. Mark the equal sides and then check which vertices lie opposite them.
mistakes: A straight line through a point does not always make \(180^\circ\) the total for every marked angle.
Vertically opposite angles sit across the intersection. They do not share an arm.
The angle between the equal sides is the apex angle. The equal angles are at the other two vertices.

examples.title: Apply the correct line or point angle fact
examples.question: The horizontal line is straight. Find x.
examples.solution:
Angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

\(180^\circ-37^\circ=143^\circ\).

examples.title: Apply the correct line or point angle fact
examples.question: The two intersecting lines are straight. Find x.
examples.solution:
Vertically opposite angles are equal.

\(x=37^\circ\).

examples.title: Find a base angle in an isosceles triangle
examples.question: Triangle ABC has AB = AC and \(\angle BAC\) = \(36^\circ\). Find \(\angle ABC\).
examples.solution:
The base angles opposite the two equal sides are equal.

Subtract \(36^\circ\) from \(180^\circ\) and share the result equally to obtain \(72^\circ\).

lessons.title: Angles in parallel lines
lessons.summary: Identify corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles and use the correct reasons.
lessons.objective: Identify corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles and use the correct reasons.
lessons.before: Look for matching arrow marks that indicate parallel sides.
lessons.ideas:
If the crossed lines are parallel, corresponding angles are equal. Follow the same side of the transversal and the same side of each parallel line.

Alternate angles are equal when the lines are parallel. If a diagram is rotated, the side relationship still identifies the pair.

When several facts are needed, find one labelled angle first. Then use equality or the straight-line sum to reach the target.
lessons.method:
Which angles occupy the matching corner?

A transversal crosses two lines. Corresponding angles are in the same relative corner at the two crossings.

Which interior angles lie on opposite sides?

Interior angles lie between the parallel lines. An alternate pair is on opposite sides of the transversal at different crossings.

When do the interior angles total 180°?

Co-interior angles are between the parallels on the same side of the transversal. Their sizes add to \(180^\circ\).
mistakes: Two angles with similar drawn sizes are not a reason for equality. Use the stated parallel lines and the angle positions.
Looking for a remembered letter shape can obscure the relevant lines. Check the actual centre points and sides of the transversal.
Co-interior angles generally differ in size. The shared result is their sum, not equality.

examples.title: Use a marked pair of angles in parallel lines
examples.question: The two horizontal lines are parallel. Find x and use the marked angles.
examples.solution:
Corresponding angles in parallel lines are equal.

The marked angle is \(47^\circ\).

examples.title: Use a marked pair of angles in parallel lines
examples.question: The two horizontal lines are parallel. Find x and use the marked angles.
examples.solution:
Co-interior angles in parallel lines sum to 180°.

The marked angle is \(133^\circ\).

examples.title: Know when parallel-angle rules apply
examples.question:
Two straight lines are crossed by a transversal. One angle is \(47^\circ\). The two lines are not known to be parallel. Can you conclude its corresponding angle is the same?

  1. No, the lines must be established as parallel
  2. Yes, every corresponding pair is equal
  3. Yes, angles are always equal if they lie on two lines
examples.solution:
Corresponding and alternate equalities used here need parallel lines.

The position of two angles alone does not establish equality.

lessons.title: Interior and exterior angles in polygons
lessons.summary: Find angle sums and side counts of regular polygons, with irregular polygons in the Extended section.
lessons.objective: Find angle sums and side counts of regular polygons, with irregular polygons in the Extended section.
lessons.before: Recall the interior angle sum of a triangle and the size of one complete turn.
lessons.ideas:
In a regular \(n\)-sided polygon all these exterior turns are equal. Each is \(\frac{360^\circ}{n}\). If you know the exterior angle, divide the full turn by that angle to find the side count.

To recover the side count from an interior angle, subtract it from \(180^\circ\) first. Use the exterior turn in the division by \(360^\circ\).

The interior angle sum of a simple \(n\)-sided polygon is \(180^\circ(n-2)\). In an irregular polygon, subtract the known individual angles from the total. Equality of all angles is a property of a regular polygon.
lessons.method:
Why do the exterior turns make one full turn?

As you walk round a convex polygon, turn at each corner until facing along its next side. Back at the start, the total outside turn is \(360^\circ\).

How does an exterior turn give an interior angle?

At a convex vertex, the interior angle and its exterior turn make a straight angle. Find one by subtracting the other from \(180^\circ\).

What if the interior angles are different?

Cut a convex polygon into triangles by drawing its diagonals from one vertex. It makes \(n-2\) triangles.
mistakes: The exterior angle used here is the turn at the boundary. It is not the large reflex angle outside the polygon.
Dividing \(360^\circ\) by an interior angle usually gives the wrong side count.
An irregular polygon can have unequal angles even if some of its sides match. Dividing the total by the side count gives their mean and may not give any one angle.

examples.title: Find a regular polygon's exterior angle
examples.question: Find one exterior turning angle of a regular polygon with 5 sides.
examples.solution:
One full circuit turns through 360°. The equal exterior turns share this total.

Divide \(360^\circ\) by 5. The angle is \(72^\circ\).

examples.title: Recover the number of sides from an angle
examples.question: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is \(72^\circ\). How many sides does it have?
examples.solution:
The exterior turning angle is \(72^\circ\).

Divide \(360^\circ\) by \(72^\circ\) to obtain 5 sides.

examples.title: Use triangulation for the interior angle sum
examples.question: Find the sum of the interior angles of a polygon with 5 sides.
examples.solution:
A convex 5-sided polygon can be split into 3 triangles from one vertex.

Multiply 3 by \(180^\circ\) to get \(540^\circ\).

lessons.title: Angles in semicircles and at tangents
lessons.summary: Use the two Core circle rules and combine them with triangle facts.
lessons.objective: Use the two Core circle rules and combine them with triangle facts.
lessons.before: Identify a diameter, a radius and a tangent from the geometry markings.
lessons.ideas:
Name the rule ‘angle in a semicircle’. An angle at the centre or at a diameter endpoint is a different angle.

At the contact point, the tangent and the radius are perpendicular. When they form part of a triangle, mark the right angle and use the triangle angle sum.

Find an angle using the tangent-radius right angle or the semicircle rule first. Then use equal base angles or the triangle angle sum to reach the next angle.
lessons.method:
Which angle made by a diameter is a right angle?

Place the endpoints of a diameter at A and B. If C is another point on the circle, the lines CA and CB form a right angle at C.

Where is the radius perpendicular to the tangent?

A tangent touches the circle at a single point. Draw the radius from the centre to that point of contact.

How do equal radii help in a circle triangle?

Each radius has the same length. Two radii to distinct points form two equal sides of an isosceles triangle.
mistakes: A straight line joining two circle points is only a diameter if it passes through the centre.
A radius drawn to a different point on the circle does not necessarily meet the same tangent at a right angle.
Do not jump straight to a result measured from the sketch. Give the circle fact and the triangle fact separately.

examples.title: Spot the angle made by a diameter
examples.question: A, B and C lie on a circle, and AB is a diameter. Find \(\angle ACB\).
examples.solution:
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

The angle with vertex C is \(90^\circ\).

examples.title: Identify the tangent-radius right angle
examples.question: OA is a radius and AP is a tangent touching at A. Find \(\angle OAP\).
examples.solution:
The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

The required angle is \(90^\circ\).

examples.title: Use equal radii inside a tangent diagram
examples.question: OA and OB are radii. The tangent at A contains point P. Given \(\angle PAB\) = \(28^\circ\), find \(\angle OBA\).
examples.solution:
Radius OA and tangent AP form a right angle. Equal radii make triangle AOB isosceles.

\(\angle OAB\) is \(90^\circ\) minus \(28^\circ\), which gives \(62^\circ\) at each base corner.

lessons.title: Circle angle theorems I (Extended)
lessons.summary: Use centre and circumference, same segment, cyclic quadrilateral and alternate segment theorems.
lessons.objective: Use centre and circumference, same segment, cyclic quadrilateral and alternate segment theorems.
lessons.before: Expect to give a named geometric reason with every calculated angle.
lessons.ideas:
The centre angle subtending that same arc is twice the circumference angle. If the circumference angle is obtuse, the matching centre angle is reflex.

Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to \(180^\circ\). This applies to four points on a single circle. Find the two opposite vertices before using it.

Identify the endpoints of the chord and the correct tangent ray. Then find the vertex in the opposite segment. Combine with the tangent-radius right angle when a remaining piece is required.
lessons.method:
Which central angle is twice the angle at the circumference?

Take the endpoints of the arc from the two arms of the circumference angle. The relevant arc between them does not contain the angle's vertex.

How do I choose between equality and a 180° sum?

Angles subtended by the same chord are equal in the same segment. Their vertices lie on the same side of the chord.

How does a tangent angle relate to a circle angle?

At the contact point, the angle between a tangent and a chord matches the angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment.
mistakes: The smaller angle at the centre is not always the one subtending the same arc.
Angles on different sides of a chord are not the same-segment pair. Treat the actual arrangement of the four points.
A chord different from the one forming the tangent angle gives a different circle angle.

examples.title: Compare a centre angle with the circumference angle
examples.question: O is the centre. The angle \(\angle ACB\) on the circle is \(29^\circ\). Find the smaller angle \(\angle AOB\) subtended by the same arc AB.
examples.solution:
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.

The central angle on the specified arc is twice \(29^\circ\), so it is \(58^\circ\).

examples.title: Use angles in the same segment
examples.question: A, B, C and D lie on the circle. C and D are on the same side of chord AB. If \(\angle ACB\) = \(29^\circ\), find \(\angle ADB\).
examples.solution:
Angles in the same segment standing on the same chord are equal.

\(\angle ADB\) is \(29^\circ\).

examples.title: Use the alternate segment theorem
examples.question: AP is tangent at A and B and C lie on the circle. The angle \(\angle PAB\) is \(29^\circ\). Find \(\angle ACB\).
examples.solution:
The angle between the tangent and chord equals the angle subtended by that chord in the alternate segment.

The angle in the opposite segment is \(29^\circ\).

lessons.title: Circle symmetry theorems II (Extended)
lessons.summary: Use equal chords, perpendicular bisectors and equal tangents to determine lengths and locate the centre.
lessons.objective: Use equal chords, perpendicular bisectors and equal tangents to determine lengths and locate the centre.
lessons.before: A point-to-line distance is measured along a perpendicular. All radii of one circle are equal.
lessons.ideas:
Equal chords in the same circle have equal perpendicular distances from the centre. They can lie on different sides of the centre and at different orientations.

Join the centre to one endpoint. The radius, the distance to the chord and the half-chord make a right triangle. Find the half-length first, then double it if the full chord is requested.

If the lengths are written as expressions, equate them and solve. A radius also meets its tangent at right angles at the contact. Use that right triangle to find one length if required.
lessons.method:
How do I compare two chords' distances from the centre?

The distance from the centre to a chord is measured along a line at right angles to that chord.

How does the perpendicular from the centre divide a chord?

The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre. Conversely the perpendicular from the centre to a chord ends at its midpoint.

What does a shared external start tell me about tangent lengths?

The two tangents drawn from the same external point to a circle have equal lengths up to their contacts.
mistakes: A sloping line joining the centre to an endpoint is a radius. It is not the perpendicular distance to the chord.
A right triangle involving the perpendicular contains only half of the chord, even when the question gives or asks for the full length.
Equal lengths follow from the common external start. Tangents from different start points need not have the same length.

examples.title: Use equal chords to compare distances from the centre
examples.question: Two chords have equal lengths. The perpendicular distance from the centre to the first chord is 2 cm. Find the perpendicular distance to the second.
examples.solution:
The relevant distance from a point to a line is measured along a perpendicular.

Equal chords are equidistant from the centre, so the second distance is \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\).

examples.title: Locate the centre from a chord's perpendicular bisector
examples.question:
A chord is 6 cm long. M is its midpoint. On which line must the centre O lie?

  1. The line through M perpendicular to the chord
  2. The chord itself for every chord
  3. Any line through M
examples.solution:
O is equally far from both ends of the chord because those distances are equal radii.

Points equally distant from the two endpoints lie on the perpendicular bisector.

examples.title: Use the equality of two tangents from one point
examples.question: PA and PB are tangents from an external point P. Their lengths in centimetres are \(3x+3\) and \(x+9\). Find x.
examples.solution:
Tangents from the same external point have equal lengths. So \(3x+3=x+9\).

Collect x-terms and constants. This gives \(x=3\).

questions.title: Find the length scale factor in the required direction
questions.prompt_html: Corresponding sides of small and large similar shapes are 18 cm and 24 cm. Find the length scale factor from small to large.
questions.solution_html:
Put the target length above the starting length. The ratio is \(\frac{24}{18}\)=\(\frac{4}{3}\).

The factor is greater than one because the target is bigger.
questions.hint_html: Put the length in the target shape over the matching start length.

The factor is greater than one because the target is bigger.
questions.hint_html: Put the length in the target shape over the matching start length.

questions.title: Find a missing length in a larger similar triangle
questions.prompt_html: Two similar triangles have corresponding bases 18 cm and 24 cm. A different small side is 24 cm. Find the matching large side.
questions.solution_html:
The enlargement multiplies lengths by \(\frac{4}{3}\).

Multiply \(24\) by that factor to get \(32\,\mathrm{cm}\).
questions.hint_html: Use one pair to find the factor, and apply it to the other pair.

questions.hint_html: Use one pair to find the factor, and apply it to the other pair.

questions.title: Find the matching shorter side
questions.prompt_html: In two similar triangles the large base is 24 cm and the matching small base is 18 cm. Another large side is 32 cm. Find the matching small side.
questions.solution_html:
The larger triangle is \(\frac{4}{3}\) times the smaller one.

Divide the known large side by \(\frac{4}{3}\). The small side is \(24\,\mathrm{cm}\).
questions.hint_html: The question goes from the large shape back to the small one.

1. The two intersecting lines are straight. Find x.

    Show the readings or working used.

    [2]

  2. In triangle ABC, \(\angle BAC\) is \(62^\circ\) and \(\angle ABC\) is \(57^\circ\). Find \(\angle BCA\).

    Show the readings or working used.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:

Vertically opposite angles are equal.

\(180^\circ-62^\circ-57^\circ=61^\circ\).

(b) The middle letter tells you which corner each angle is at.

questions.title: Explain when equal-angle rules apply
questions.prompt_html:
1. Two corresponding angles on parallel lines are \((2x+5)^\circ\) and \(59^\circ\). Find x.

    Show the readings or working used.

    [2]

  2. Two straight lines are crossed by a transversal. One angle is \(81^\circ\). The two lines are not known to be parallel. Can you conclude its corresponding angle is the same?

    1. Yes, angles are always equal if they lie on two lines
    2. No, the lines must be established as parallel
    3. Yes, every corresponding pair is equal

    Show the readings or working used.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(27\)

(b) No, the lines must be established as parallel
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Corresponding angles are equal, so \(2x+5=59\).

Subtract 5 and divide by 2 to get \(x=27\).

Corresponding and alternate equalities used here need parallel lines.

The position of two angles alone does not establish equality.

1. OA and OB are radii. The tangent at A contains point P. Given \(\angle PAB\) = \(56^\circ\), find \(\angle OBA\).

    Show the readings or working used.

    [2]

  2. A, B and C are points on the same circle. Which fact is enough to make \(\angle ACB\) a right angle?

    1. Any radius drawn to the vertex
    2. A diameter at the endpoints of the angle's arms
    3. Any chord joining the endpoints

    Show the readings or working used.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(34^\circ\)

(b) A diameter at the endpoints of the angle's arms
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Radius OA and tangent AP form a right angle. Equal radii make triangle AOB isosceles.

\(\angle OAB\) is \(90^\circ\) minus \(56^\circ\), which gives \(34^\circ\) at each base corner.

(b)

The points A and B must be the endpoints of a diameter for this rule.

At C, the angle subtended by that diameter is a right angle.
questions.hint_html:
(a) Work from the tangent-radius right angle to the angle inside the isosceles triangle.

(b) An ordinary chord might not go through the centre.

marking_criteria.description_html: Radius OA and tangent AP form a right angle. Equal radii make triangle AOB isosceles.
Name the exact diameter condition for the angle in a semicircle.
Give the complete result. A diameter at the endpoints of the angle's arms

questions.title: Compare a centre angle with the circumference angle
questions.prompt_html: O is the centre. The angle \(\angle ACB\) on the circle is \(46^\circ\). Find the smaller angle \(\angle AOB\) subtended by the same arc AB.
questions.solution_html:
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.

The central angle on the specified arc is twice \(46^\circ\), so it is \(92^\circ\).

questions.title: Connect the alternate segment theorem with a right angle
questions.prompt_html: AP is tangent at A, O is the centre, and B and C lie on the circle. Given \(\angle ACB\) = \(46^\circ\), find \(\angle OAB\).
questions.solution_html:
Use the alternate segment theorem for the tangent and chord AB. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at A.

\(\angle PAB\) is \(46^\circ\). The remaining part of the right angle \(\angle OAP\) is \(44^\circ\).
